narrativeReportMd:
# instant R4 to R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
One local hard instance-breaking change was found: R6 narrows the `instant.value` lexical regex so fractional seconds may contain at most 9 digits. R4 allowed one or more fractional-second digits with no explicit upper bound.

## Scope
The report analyzes the core `instant` primitive datatype StructureDefinition in R4 and the R6 ballot build. The R6 artifact is present at the same canonical URL. The R4 base `Element` to R6 base `PrimitiveType` hierarchy shift is intentionally treated as inherited infrastructure scope, not as a local `instant` finding.

## Main migration themes
The only material local migration theme is precision normalization. Existing R4 data that carries more than nanosecond precision in an `instant` can fail R6 validation. R6-valid `instant` values remain representable in R4 because the R6 fractional-second form is a subset of the R4 regex.

## Highest-impact findings
`instant:VALUE_CONSTRAINT:instant.value:fractional-seconds-9digits` is a direct R4-to-R6 validation break for values such as `2020-01-01T00:00:00.1234567890Z`.

## Findings requiring human review
No finding requires human review for the existence of the delta; the regex change is explicit in the StructureDefinitions. Human policy may still be needed to decide whether to round, truncate, reject, or preserve extra precision during migration.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The precision cap is probably intended to align the primitive with interoperable timestamp precision, but no official change rationale was available. A less-breaking alternative would have preserved the R4 regex and introduced a warning, guidance, or profile-level constraint.

## Follow-up analysis
Base datatype hierarchy changes involving `PrimitiveType`, `DataType`, and `Element` should be assessed in the corresponding base-artifact reports.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: R6 keeps `instant` at the same canonical identity but narrows the primitive value regex to at most 9 fractional-second digits. This is a hard R4-to-R6 validation break for over-9-digit fractional instants; the main uncertainty is the uninspected official rationale, not the existence of the change.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should scan every `instant`-typed value for fractional seconds longer than 9 digits. R4 values at second precision or with 1-9 fractional digits should continue to validate lexically in R6. Values with greater precision require an explicit policy: round, truncate, reject, or preserve the original string outside the base primitive through an extension or audit trail.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for the computable delta because both StructureDefinitions are present and the regex difference is explicit in `instant.value`. Confidence is lower for the design justification because no official diff, ballot issue, or narrative page explaining the cap was supplied.

findings.title: instant.value fractional-second precision narrowed to 1-9 digits

oldState.summary: R4 allowed any positive number of fractional-second digits when a fractional part is present.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 regex fragment for the optional fractional component is `(\.[0-9]+)?`, so an `instant` with 10, 12, or more fractional-second digits can satisfy the base lexical pattern as long as the rest of the timestamp is valid and includes `Z` or an offset.

newState.summary: R6 allows only 1 through 9 fractional-second digits when a fractional part is present.
newState.narrativeMd: The R6 regex fragment is `(\.[0-9]{1,9})?`, which caps fractional precision at 9 digits. Seconds, offset syntax, leap-second allowance, date bounds, and the FHIRPath type remain otherwise unchanged for this local element.

facts.note: The optional fractional seconds component changed from unbounded one-or-more digits to a bounded 1-9 digit range.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged (`instant.value`), and the only local value-domain delta is the regex extension on the same type entry.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break. An R4-valid `instant` with more than 9 fractional-second digits matches the R4 regex but fails the R6 regex. Runtime risk is medium because strict validators, generated schemas, and parsers that enforce the R6 primitive regex will reject such values, but over-9-digit precision is not expected to be the common case. R6-to-R4 representability risk is informational because every R6-valid fractional precision allowed by this regex is also allowed by the broader R4 regex.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The main business risk is migration or ingestion failure for audit/log timestamps with unusually high precision. No direct clinical safety issue was identified from the datatype definition alone.

justification.inferredGoal: Limit instant precision to an interoperable maximum, likely nanosecond precision, while preserving required seconds and timezone/offset syntax.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 unbounded fractional-second regex in the base datatype and add a base warning, best-practice rule, documentation, or profile-level cap recommending at most 9 digits.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal appears reasonable: capping `instant` fractional seconds at 9 digits creates a clear nanosecond-scale interoperability boundary for a primitive intended for precise machine-observed timestamps. The break is real but narrow: only R4 values with more than 9 fractional digits are rejected, while common second and subsecond forms remain valid. Because a less-breaking base design could only encourage or profile the cap without making all base R6 `instant` values bounded, the material tradeoff supports `Probably justified` rather than `Not clearly justified`.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep the R4 lexical form `(\.[0-9]+)?` and add non-fatal base guidance such as a warning invariant or best-practice statement that producers SHOULD limit fractional seconds to 9 digits, with stricter profiles for systems requiring nanosecond-compatible storage. That is a real base-design alternative, not just migration tooling, because it would preserve existing R4-valid instances. It is only partial: it would leave duplicate conformance expectations, validation ambiguity, and ongoing interoperability cost for implementations that need a hard maximum.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve R4 data but would not guarantee a bounded base R6 value space; systems could keep producing over-9-digit instants that many implementations cannot store, compare, or round-trip consistently.

evidence.detail: R4 regex uses an unbounded fractional-second fragment.
R6 regex caps the fractional-second fragment at 1-9 digits.

examples.examplesMd: The example is a datatype fragment showing the relevant lexical issue, not a complete resource. The input has 10 fractional-second digits: valid under the R4 regex fragment `+`, invalid under the R6 `{1,9}` cap. Rounding or truncation must be a deliberate business decision because it may lose precision.

findings.narrativeMd: `instant.value` keeps the same element identity, cardinality, and FHIRPath type, but its lexical value space is narrowed. R4 accepted fractional seconds of arbitrary length; R6 accepts at most 9 digits. Implementers migrating historical logs, audit timestamps, or high-precision machine-generated instants can therefore encounter records that were valid in R4 but fail base R6 primitive validation.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is affected: a value such as `2020-01-01T00:00:00.1234567890Z` matches the R4 primitive regex and fails the R6 regex. R6-to-R4 conversion is not materially affected by this specific narrowing because R4 accepts all R6-permitted fractional precisions. Strict parsers, generated regex validators, JSON/XML schema validators, and FHIRPath-aware validation code are the likely enforcement points.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all `instant`-typed fields and test values with more than 9 fractional-second digits. Choose and document a deterministic policy: reject the record, round to 9 digits, truncate to 9 digits, or preserve the original lexical value in an extension or audit store while using an R6-valid normalized value. Regression tests should include no fractional part, 1 digit, 9 digits, and 10 digits.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been made less disruptive by retaining the R4 regex in the base datatype and expressing the 9-digit cap as guidance, a warning invariant, or profile-level rule. That would have preserved old instances but weakened the guarantee that all base R6 `instant` values fit within the desired precision envelope.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 keeps the `instant.value` path and primitive shape but narrows the lexical value space from arbitrary fractional-second length to at most 9 digits. A concrete R4 payload such as an audit or device-generated instant with 10 fractional digits is valid against the R4 regex and invalid against the R6 regex. The affected content is normative and this primitive is reused wherever `instant` appears, so even if over-9-digit precision is probably uncommon, the hard validation break needs a clear standards rationale and migration policy before it should be considered acceptable.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-instant.json snapshot `instant.value` regex contains `(\.[0-9]+)?`, allowing any positive fractional-second length.
R6 StructureDefinition-instant.json snapshot `instant.value` regex contains `(\.[0-9]{1,9})?`, capping fractional seconds at 9 digits.
R4 maturity map records `instant` standardsStatus `normative` and normativeVersion `4.0.0`; the R4 and R6 StructureDefinitions also carry normative status extensions.
R6 applies the same 1-9 fractional-second cap to `dateTime.value`, `time.value`, and `instant.value`, suggesting a deliberate temporal-primitive cleanup rather than an accidental diff.
freshReview.fmmEffect: The supplied R4 maturity context is normative, and local maturity/status evidence also shows normative status. That raises the burden of justification for a direct old-valid/new-invalid primitive value-space narrowing, even if the affected precision range is likely low-prevalence.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances with `instant` values containing more than 9 fractional-second digits pass the R4 primitive regex but fail the R6 primitive regex; strict validators, schemas, and parsers enforcing R6 lexical rules can reject them.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design appears plausible: retain the R4 unbounded fractional-second regex for base validity while adding normative guidance, a warning-level invariant, or implementation support expectations that recommend no more than 9 digits. That would preserve old data and still improve interoperability guidance, but it would not give R6 the same hard bounded-precision guarantee and could leave arbitrary-precision handling burdens on implementations.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly identifies a hard R4-to-R6 validation break and high concern for normative content, but it does not give enough weight to the plausible less-breaking base design or the need for explicit rationale for this normative narrowing.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The R6 artifact has the same id, canonical URL, name, kind, and type as R4. The base-definition shift is recorded but excluded as inherited infrastructure scope.
The local snapshot still contains `instant`, `instant.id`, `instant.extension`, and `instant.value`; no local elements were added, removed, renamed, moved, split, or merged.
`instant.value` remains `http://hl7.org/fhirpath/System.DateTime` with FHIR type `instant`; no choice type or datatype replacement was found.
`instant` has no Reference-typed elements or targetProfiles.
`instant` has no terminology bindings or value sets.

No local ElementDefinition.constraint expression introduced a material validation change. The inherited `ele-1` expression remains equivalent in the instant snapshot; XPath metadata removal is treated as inherited/tooling scope. The regex value-domain change is reported separately as a value constraint finding.
No fixed value, pattern, or default value was found on `instant` or `instant.value`.
`isModifier` remains false for the visible `instant` elements.
`isSummary` remains false for the visible `instant` elements.
No local slicing was introduced on `instant.value`. Inherited extension slicing belongs to base artifacts.

The root comment changed from `Time zone is always required` to `UTC offset is always required`, which appears to clarify the same regex requirement for `Z` or an offset. Human-authored narrative pages could improve confidence in the intended semantic nuance.
The XML attribute representation for `instant.value` remains present. No JSON/XML structural serialization change was found apart from the lexical regex narrowing reported as a finding.
The R6 local value domain for fractional seconds is a subset of R4's local value domain, and no new local element needs down-conversion.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds type-characteristic metadata for range, continuity, and length
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds `structuredefinition-type-characteristics` extensions with `has-range`, `is-continuous`, and `has-length`. These are metadata additions and do not by themselves invalidate R4 instances or require a different serialized representation.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology, validation, and code-generation tooling may expose these traits for sorting, range comparisons, or length-aware behavior. Treat them as additive metadata unless a profile or implementation guide makes them operational.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Root comment now says UTC offset is required
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R4 said `Time zone is always required`; R6 says `UTC offset is always required`. The regex in both versions requires either `Z` or an explicit numeric offset, so this appears to clarify terminology rather than change valid offset forms.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Review user-facing documentation and validation messages that copied the older phrase, but no instance transform is needed for this prose-only clarification.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 introduces `PrimitiveType` as the base for `instant` while R4 `instant` specialized `Element`. Per scope rules, hierarchy and inherited content-model implications should be assessed in the `PrimitiveType`, `DataType`, and `Element` base-artifact reports rather than duplicated here.
